notes.b: The Earth is kept warm by gases in the atmosphere that act a little like the glass of a greenhouse. The effect works in four steps, and it is the basis for everything else about climate change.
points: 1. Sunlight, which is mostly visible and short-wave radiation, passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
2. The warm surface gives off long-wave infrared radiation, which is heat, back towards space.
3. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere (water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide) absorb some of this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back down to the surface.
4. As a result, the lower atmosphere and the surface are warmer than they would otherwise be, because some of the heat that would have escaped is returned to the surface.
The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life: without it the Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C, which is too cold for most life.
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the extra warming caused by human increases in greenhouse gases, on top of the natural effect.

Climate change is the long-term change in the Earth's climate, including temperature, rainfall and extreme weather, and it is now driven mainly by the enhanced greenhouse effect. Global warming is the rise in average surface temperature, which is only one part of climate change.

Diagram: the greenhouse effect. Draw the Sun, the Earth's surface and a layer of greenhouse gases. Show incoming sunlight passing through, outgoing infrared, some infrared escaping to space and some re-emitted back to the surface. Label sunlight, infrared (heat), greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄).
notes.tip: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared (heat) coming from the Earth, not incoming sunlight, so never say they trap the Sun's rays. The greenhouse effect is also a separate matter from the hole in the ozone layer, so do not link them.

notes.h: Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
notes.b: Three gases made or released by living things and human farming add most to the enhanced greenhouse effect. They differ in how much is released, how strongly each warms the air and how long it lasts.
points: Carbon dioxide: atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 parts per million today. This comes mainly from burning fossil fuels and from deforestation. There is more on this in The carbon cycle.
CO₂ is the largest single cause of human-caused warming because so much of it is released and it stays in the atmosphere for centuries.
Methane (CH₄): its concentration has more than doubled since before the Industrial Revolution.

Methane sources include anaerobic microorganisms (archaea, which live without oxygen) in the stomachs (rumens) of cattle and sheep, released mainly by belching; manure and slurry stores; rice paddies; landfill sites; natural wetlands and bogs; and leaks from natural-gas wells and pipelines.
Kilogram for kilogram, methane traps far more heat than CO₂: over 100 years about 30 times as much, and over 20 years about 80 times as much. Note that this is per kilogram, not per molecule.
Methane lasts only about 12 years in the air before it is broken down to CO₂, whereas CO₂ persists for centuries. So cutting methane slows warming quickly.

Nitrous oxide (N₂O) comes from fertilised and waterlogged soils and from manure, where it is formed by denitrification (bacteria turning nitrate into gases). It is a third biological greenhouse gas, and kilogram for kilogram it is about 270 times as powerful as CO₂ over 100 years.
notes.tip: Cattle methane comes mainly from belching by rumen microorganisms, not mainly from flatulence or manure. Do not just say methane is worse than CO₂: say it is stronger per kilogram but breaks down within about 12 years, while CO₂ lasts for centuries.

notes.b: Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions have an unusual pattern, because farming rather than transport or industry is the biggest source. The law sets targets that farming must also meet.
points: Agriculture is the largest single source of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly methane from cattle and nitrous oxide from fertiliser and manure, because Ireland has a large, grass-fed cattle herd.

Ireland's law, the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021, sets a 51% cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 2018, and climate neutrality by 2050. Agriculture's own target is a 25% cut by 2030.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name sources of methane, especially in Irish agriculture. Link the cattle herd to rumen microorganisms and slurry, and the fertiliser to nitrous oxide.

notes.h: Evidence linking greenhouse gases to warming
notes.b: Scientists do not rely on one observation. Several independent lines of evidence show that rising greenhouse gases are the cause of recent warming, and governments have responded to them.
points: Evidence: greenhouse gases absorb infrared, a property measured in the laboratory since the nineteenth century, so the mechanism is known.
Evidence: direct measurements show CO₂ and methane rising together with global temperature.
Evidence: air bubbles trapped in ancient ice cores show that CO₂ and temperature rose and fell together over hundreds of thousands of years.

Evidence: the observed warming pattern, in which the lower atmosphere warms while the upper atmosphere cools, fits greenhouse gases and not a brighter Sun, because a brighter Sun would warm every layer.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) concluded in 2021 that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the climate, by about 1.1 °C for 2011–2020 compared with 1850–1900.
The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. There is more on scientific consensus in Evaluating evidence.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss the link between CO₂, methane and climate change, give the mechanism (infrared absorption) and at least one line of evidence such as ice cores or the warming pattern.

notes.b: Good scientific discussion also says what is less certain. Warming can also set off feedbacks, where the effect of warming makes more warming more likely.
points: Uncertainty: correlation alone does not prove cause. Here the physics of infrared absorption supplies the mechanism.
Uncertainty: exactly how much warming a given rise in CO₂ causes, and how regional rainfall will change, are less certain than the direction of change, because feedbacks are hard to model.
Feedback: warming speeds up decomposition by soil microorganisms, releasing more CO₂, which causes further warming. There is more on this in The microbiome.
Feedback: thawing permafrost, which is frozen soil in the Arctic, lets stored organic matter decompose, releasing CO₂ and methane.
Feedback: warmer oceans dissolve less CO₂, so more stays in the air.
Feedback: drought and fires turn forests from sinks (stores that take in more carbon than they release) into sources.

notes.b: Climate change matters biologically because living things are adapted to particular temperatures, seasons and chemistry. Each of these changes has its own effect.
points: Species' ranges move towards the poles or uphill to stay cool, and species that cannot move or adapt face extinction. There is more on this in Biodiversity loss and conservation.
The timing of events such as flowering, breeding and migration changes, so species may get out of step with their food.
More CO₂ dissolving in the oceans makes them more acidic (ocean acidification), which makes it harder for corals, shellfish and some phytoplankton to build calcium carbonate shells.
Warmer seas cause coral bleaching.
Insects that spread disease can spread to new areas as temperatures rise. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.

notes.h: Carbon sinks: plants, algae and phytoplankton
notes.b: A carbon sink takes in more carbon than it releases. Living photosynthesisers on land and in the sea are the biological sinks, and they differ in how long they hold the carbon.
points: Forests and other land plants: trees store carbon in wood for decades or centuries, and in roots and soil. The sink is strong while trees grow. A mature forest takes in roughly what it releases.
The store in a forest is lost quickly if the forest burns, dies or is felled, because the carbon returns to the air as CO₂.
Phytoplankton and algae: microscopic algae and cyanobacteria in the oceans carry out about half of all photosynthesis on Earth.
When phytoplankton die or are eaten, some of their carbon sinks to the deep ocean and sea floor, which is called the biological pump. There it can stay for centuries or longer.
Seaweeds such as kelp, and seagrass meadows and saltmarshes, also store carbon, which is called blue carbon.
notes.tip: Name the sink and say how it removes or stores carbon: photosynthesis fixes it, then wood, peat or sinking dead matter holds it. Do not claim trees or any one sink can offset all emissions.

notes.b: Some of the biggest stores of carbon are not living plants at all but waterlogged peat and soil, where dead plant matter has built up.
points: Bogs and other peatlands: waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen conditions stop decomposition, so a healthy bog accumulates peat (partly rotted plant matter) very slowly over thousands of years.
Peatlands cover only about 3% of the world's land but hold more carbon than all the world's forests. A bog is a sink only while it stays wet.

Soils: soil organic matter (humus) stores more carbon than all plants and the atmosphere together. Grassland and undisturbed soils keep it, while ploughing and draining release it because air reaches the organic matter and it decomposes.

notes.b: The sinks differ in how fast they take up carbon, how much they hold and how securely. Comparing them shows why none of them is enough on its own.
points: Bogs store the most carbon per hectare and for the longest time, but gain it very slowly. Forests take up carbon fastest but store it less securely. Oceans are the largest active sink, but they are becoming more acidic and absorb less as they warm.
All natural sinks together absorb only about half of the CO₂ humans release each year, so sinks can slow the rise but cannot replace cutting emissions.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name sinks and explain how each removes or stores carbon. If asked to compare, use the three measures of speed, amount per hectare and security.

notes.h: Reducing CO₂: protecting forests, bogs and wetlands
notes.b: Biological strategies for cutting atmospheric CO₂ are judged by how they work, the case for, the case against and an overall judgement. The simplest strategy is to keep the carbon already stored where it is.
points: How it works: protecting existing forests, bogs and wetlands keeps carbon in place, so it is never released.
For: it is the quickest and cheapest way to avoid emissions, with large benefits for biodiversity and water.
Against: land is valuable for farming or development, and protection needs enforcement and payment to landowners. There is more on the ethics in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
Judgement: it is the most effective first step, because it avoids emissions instead of waiting for new growth to recapture them.
notes.tip: Evaluate a named strategy with how it works, one for, one against and a judgement. Stick to biological effectiveness and mention fairness only briefly.

notes.b: Planting trees uses photosynthesis to pull CO₂ out of the air. The benefits are real, but the details of what is planted and where matter a great deal.
points: How it works: afforestation (planting new forests) and reforestation (replanting cleared land) use photosynthesis to fix CO₂ into wood.
For: they take up carbon for decades. Native broadleaved woodland also supports biodiversity, reduces flooding, and gives timber that can replace concrete and steel.
Against: they are slow, taking decades to reach full uptake. Fire, storms and disease can release the carbon, and they need land that could grow food.
Against: conifers planted on deep peat can release more carbon from the drained peat than the trees take up, because draining lets the peat decompose.
Against: dense plantations of one non-native species, in Ireland mostly Sitka spruce, support less wildlife.
Ireland's forest cover is about 11%, among the lowest in the EU.
Judgement: valuable if the right trees are planted in the right places, but slow.

notes.h: Reducing CO₂: rewetting and restoring bogs
notes.b: Ireland has drained a great deal of peat, which turns a carbon store into a CO₂ source. Putting the water back reverses this.
points: How it works: blocking drains so the water table rises. Conditions become anaerobic again, decomposition stops, and sphagnum moss starts forming peat.
For: it quickly stops the large CO₂ release from drained peat, restores rare habitat, and holds water to reduce flooding. Bord na Móna's cutaway bogs are being rewetted on a large scale.
Against: rewetted bogs give off some methane from anaerobic decomposition. New peat forms very slowly, so the gain is mainly avoided CO₂ loss rather than fast uptake.
Against: the land can no longer be used for turf or farming.
Judgement: strongly beneficial for Ireland because so much peat is drained.
notes.tip: Mention the methane trade-off: wet anaerobic conditions stop CO₂ loss but produce some methane.

notes.h: Reducing CO₂: algae, soil carbon and bioenergy
notes.b: Three further strategies use algae, soil management or plants as fuel. Each looks attractive, but each has a limit that you should be able to name.
points: Algae and phytoplankton: seaweed farming and algae grown in tanks fix CO₂ fast, and the algae can be made into food, feed or biofuel. For: algae grow much faster than land plants and need no farmland or fresh water.
Against algae: if the algae are eaten or burned, the carbon returns to the air, so the sink lasts only if the carbon is stored.

Against algae: adding iron to the ocean to cause phytoplankton blooms has been tested, but little of the carbon was shown to reach the deep ocean, and it risks harming marine ecosystems, for example by creating low-oxygen zones. It is therefore not an accepted strategy.
Judgement on algae: promising for fuels and food, but unproven as large-scale storage.

Increasing soil carbon: keeping grassland unploughed, adding manure and compost, growing cover crops over winter, reduced tillage and planting hedgerows add organic matter to soil. For: this also improves soil fertility and water-holding.
Against increasing soil carbon: soils fill up (saturate) after some decades, the gain is hard to measure, and it is lost again if the land is ploughed.

Bioenergy in place of fossil fuels: biofuels and wood or other biomass burned in power stations release CO₂ that the plants recently took in, so in principle they add little CO₂. Capturing and storing the CO₂ from burning biomass could even remove carbon.

Against bioenergy: fuel crops compete with food for land, clearing land for them releases carbon, and growing, harvesting and transporting them uses fossil fuel. So biofuels are not carbon-neutral without this qualification.
notes.tip: Never call biofuels carbon-neutral without qualification: mention land use and the fossil fuel used to grow and transport them.

notes.h: Reducing methane: cattle, livestock and diet
notes.b: Because most Irish methane comes from the rumens of cattle, the most direct strategies change what cattle eat, how they are bred, or how many there are.
points: Changes to cattle diet and breeding: feed additives (for example the chemical 3-NOP, and some seaweeds) inhibit the methane-producing microorganisms in the rumen, cutting methane in trials.
Better-quality feed and earlier finishing of cattle mean less methane per kilogram of meat or milk. Breeding cattle that naturally produce less methane is being researched.
For diet and breeding: they tackle Ireland's largest methane source directly without cutting production.

Against diet and breeding: additives are hard to give to cattle that graze outdoors for most of the year. Long-term effects and costs are still being studied. Some seaweeds contain a compound (bromoform) with health concerns, and breeding is slow.
For fewer livestock and dietary change: fewer cattle produce less methane and need less land, which could be used for forests or bogs. Eating less red meat and dairy reduces demand.

Against fewer livestock and dietary change: farming is central to Ireland's rural economy and exports. Cutting the Irish herd may only move production to countries with higher emissions per animal, which is called carbon leakage.
Against fewer livestock: meat and milk are good sources of protein, iron and calcium.
Judgement on fewer livestock and dietary change: a fair transition needs support for farmers.
notes.tip: To evaluate feed additives, say they target the rumen microorganisms and that practical limits are outdoor grazing, unknown long-term effects and cost.

notes.h: Reducing methane and nitrous oxide: digestion, waste and fertiliser
notes.b: Methane is also made in waste, and nitrous oxide comes from fertilised soil. Capturing waste methane for fuel, and cutting the gases at source, are the remaining strategies.
points: Anaerobic digestion of slurry, food waste and grass: microorganisms break down the waste without oxygen in a sealed tank, producing biogas, which is mainly methane. The biogas is burned for heat or electricity, or upgraded to replace natural gas, and the digestate (the solid left over) is used as fertiliser.
For anaerobic digestion: it captures methane that would otherwise escape from open slurry stores and landfill, replaces a fossil fuel, and recycles nutrients.
Against anaerobic digestion: the plants are expensive and leaks release methane. Burning the biogas still releases CO₂, although it is recent carbon rather than fossil carbon.
Other methods: capping landfill sites and collecting their gas; composting food waste aerobically (with oxygen) instead of sending it to landfill; reducing food waste; and covering slurry stores.
Rewetted bogs and rice paddies show that wet, anaerobic soil makes methane, which is a trade-off with storing carbon.

Nitrous oxide: using clover in grassland, applying fertiliser precisely, and using protected urea fertiliser, which releases nitrogen more slowly, all reduce nitrous oxide. They also reduce nitrate leaching. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
notes.tip: To evaluate anaerobic digestion, give the for (captures methane, replaces fossil fuel, recycles nutrients) and the against (expense, leaks, CO₂ on burning).

notes.b: A post-fossil-fuel world is one in which energy, fuels, materials and chemicals no longer come from coal, oil and gas. Biology can help by providing renewable replacements made from recently fixed carbon, and by protecting the sinks that absorb CO₂.
points: Biofuels and biogas: bioethanol is made by fermentation of sugars by yeast, and enzymes that break down cellulose for fuel help make it. There is more on this in Industrial enzymes.
Biofuels and biogas: biodiesel is made from plant oils and waste cooking oil. Biogas comes from anaerobic digestion, and fuels are also made from algae.

Bio-based materials: bioplastics are made from plant starch or sugars, such as polylactic acid (PLA), and some are biodegradable. Wood is used in construction, and plant fibres replace oil-based fibres.

Microorganisms as factories, or biomanufacturing: bacteria, yeasts and algae grown in fermenters (bioreactors) can make medicines, enzymes, food proteins and chemicals that are now made from oil. They use sugars or waste as raw materials.
Food and farming: breeding crops, including by genetic technologies, that tolerate drought, heat and new pests and need less fertiliser.
Food and farming: using legumes and soil microbiomes instead of manufactured fertiliser, which is made with fossil energy, and reducing food waste.
Biology also monitors and understands change, by measuring sinks, tracking species' ranges and predicting the spread of disease.

Limits: biomass cannot replace all fossil fuels, because land is needed for food and nature. Bio-based products are not automatically sustainable, since they depend on how the raw material is grown. Biology therefore works alongside other renewables, such as wind and solar, and alongside using less energy.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss biology's role, give examples from fuels, materials, microorganisms and farming, and finish with the limits: land is needed for food and no single answer replaces all fossil fuels.

keyTerms.definition: The warming of the lower atmosphere and surface because greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from the Earth and re-emit some of it back down.
The extra warming caused by human increases in greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
The long-term change in the Earth's climate, including temperature, rainfall and extreme weather.
The rise in average surface temperature, which is one part of climate change.
A process in which a change in the climate causes further change, such as warming releasing more CO₂ from soil.
The increase in the acidity of the oceans as they absorb more CO₂, which makes it harder for organisms to build calcium carbonate shells.
The sinking of dead phytoplankton and their carbon to the deep ocean and sea floor, where it can be stored for centuries or longer.
Carbon stored by seaweeds, seagrass meadows and saltmarshes.
Planting new forests on land that has not recently been forested.
Blocking the drains of a bog so that the water table rises, conditions become anaerobic again and peat forms.
Using bacteria, yeasts or algae grown in fermenters to make medicines, enzymes, foods and chemicals.

questions.prompt: Discuss the link between atmospheric carbon dioxide, methane and climate change.
questions.model: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the warm surface and re-emit some of it back down, so the lower atmosphere and surface are warmer than they would otherwise be. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 parts per million today, mainly from burning fossil fuels and deforestation, and it stays in the air for centuries. Methane has more than doubled in concentration, mainly from the rumens of cattle and sheep, rice paddies, landfill and wetlands. Kilogram for kilogram, methane traps far more heat than CO₂, about 30 times as much over 100 years, but it breaks down to CO₂ within about 12 years. Evidence for the link includes laboratory measurements of infrared absorption and ice cores that show CO₂ and temperature rising and falling together. One uncertainty is exactly how much warming a given rise in CO₂ causes, and how regional rainfall will change.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two biological strategies that could reduce the levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere in Ireland.
questions.model: Rewetting and restoring drained bogs works by blocking drains so that anaerobic conditions return and decomposition of peat stops. It quickly prevents the large CO₂ release from drained peat and restores rare habitat, and Bord na Móna's cutaway bogs are being rewetted on a large scale. Against it, rewetted bogs give off some methane and new peat forms very slowly, so the gain is mainly avoided loss rather than fast uptake. Judgement: it is strongly beneficial for Ireland because so much peat is drained. Anaerobic digestion of slurry and food waste works by microorganisms producing biogas, which is mainly methane, in a sealed tank. It captures methane that would otherwise escape from open slurry stores and replaces fossil fuel while recycling nutrients. Against it, the plants are expensive, leaks release methane, and burning the biogas releases CO₂. Judgement: it is a useful way to capture agricultural methane and recycle nutrients, provided that leaks are controlled and the plants are affordable.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which biology will contribute to a post-fossil-fuel world.
questions.model: Biology can provide biofuels: yeast ferment sugars to make bioethanol, which replaces petrol made from fossil fuels. Biology can also provide bio-based materials, such as bioplastics made from plant starch or sugars, which are used in place of oil-based plastics. Microorganisms grown in fermenters can also make medicines, enzymes and chemicals that are now made from oil.
